summary: AstroKinetics · ASTRA is an astronaut-health research prototype for missions with delayed Earth communications. It combines browser-based movement and pulse analysis, a 3D crew body map, emergency red-flag rules, and source-linked evidence search. An eight-signal model highlights changes from a reference baseline; four scripted mission scenarios demonstrate the workflow. A Watch + iPhone browser demo and a telemetry API show how wearable data could join the workstation. NASA OSDR OSD-571 and human-spaceflight resources provide research context. The cached core is designed for offline use; optional cloud voice services require connectivity. The prototype is not clinically validated, and native iOS/watchOS sensor capture is future work.
details:
AstroKinetics · ASTRA: From a Health Signal to an Explainable Next Step

THE CHALLENGE

Long-duration space missions require astronauts to recognize changes in their health when immediate support from Earth is unavailable. Movement changes, fatigue, environmental conditions and physiological adaptation can produce overlapping signals. A useful onboard tool must help the crew gather information, understand what changed, inspect the supporting evidence and prepare the next action.

AstroKinetics · ASTRA addresses “Create Health Monitoring Software for Astronauts on Space Missions” through a unified research prototype built by Team AI-MED 01.

HOW THE COMPONENTS COME TOGETHER

AstroKinetics provides the web workstation, camera-based movement analysis, statistical assessment and visualization. ASTRA contributes the Watch + iPhone companion experience, personal-baseline concepts and longitudinal follow-up. HUNCH-informed assessment contributes emergency red-flag patterns. AURA-derived research materials and the ASTRA knowledge library support evidence retrieval, source attribution and explanations.

These components meet in one workflow: Gather → Evaluate → Act → Follow up. The goal is to connect an observation to its context, supporting sources and next step.

1. GATHER: CAMERA, TELEMETRY AND CREW INPUT

The workstation uses browser-based MediaPipe face, body and hand landmarks to support movement analysis, experimental contactless pulse estimation and tremor-related measurements. Camera processing is implemented on the device.

A REST telemetry endpoint provides an integration point for wearable, phone and habitat measurements. The Watch + iPhone browser demonstration shows how a personal baseline, reminders and follow-up could work across devices.

The submitted build contains the web application and telemetry API. Native iOS/watchOS applications and end-to-end HealthKit capture are future integration work. Guided-demo crew values are illustrative.

2. VISUALIZE: ONE CREW BODY MAP

A 3D anatomical Crew Body Map brings measurements into a shared visual context. Users can inspect anatomical systems, sensor callouts and illustrative pulse-wave and gravity-related fluid-shift views.

The anatomy comes from BodyParts3D, with attribution and its original license preserved. These views explain concepts; they are not personalized physiological simulations or a reconstruction of the astronaut’s body.

3. EVALUATE: RED FLAGS FIRST, THEN EXPLAINABLE DEVIATION

An eight-pattern emergency red-flag gate precedes an eight-signal statistical comparison with a reference baseline. The interface exposes how individual variables contribute to the overall deviation.

Four scripted mission scenarios demonstrate nominal operation, cabin CO2 drift, movement asymmetry and a solar-particle-event scenario. Their readiness scores are example outputs, not measurements of diagnostic accuracy. Statistical contributions do not establish the medical cause of a change.

The optional conversational assistant explains and navigates the interface; it does not determine the rule-based triage result.

4. ACT AND FOLLOW UP

The prototype presents source-linked candidate actions, tracks follow-up episodes and demonstrates experimental audio cues. Its interaction design distinguishes events that should not be confused: dismissing a reminder is not completing a task, a failed capture is not a normal result, and synchronization is not a human review.

These features demonstrate a possible crew-support workflow. Clinical recommendations, thresholds and therapeutic effects require independent validation.

NASA DATA AND HOW WE USE IT

NASA Open Science Data Repository, OSD-571:

The application includes 14 selected biomarkers from the Inspiration4 profiling study. The bundled provenance records the source file and six pre-flight/post-flight visits. This supports exploration of flight-associated molecular changes. It does not establish that a camera or watch can diagnose radiation injury.

NASA-STD-3001, Volumes 1 and 2:

These resources inform the crew-health, environmental and operational context of the prototype. Referencing the standards does not imply NASA certification or compliance validation.

NASA Human Research Program and Human Research Roadmap:

These resources frame the health risks and evidence needs associated with long-duration exploration.

NASA RadLab:

An ISS DosTel sample illustrates radiation telemetry and provides an example of traceable environmental data.

NASA Life Sciences Data Archive and published sleep-study tables:

The evidence assets distinguish dataset references, published findings and illustrative values. They are not presented as private clinical records collected by our team.

The bundled knowledge library contains 16 concepts, 70 source records, 15 device-study records and 572 space-biology publication records, including 45 richer extractions. Sources retain limitations and study-population context so findings from different settings are not treated as equivalent clinical evidence.

WHAT MAKES THE PROJECT CREATIVE

The integration connects camera observations, a wearable-companion concept, an anatomical body map, transparent statistical deviation and cited evidence within the same experience.

Its distinctive contribution is the continuity between a signal, its explanation and follow-up. Users can move from “something changed” to “these variables contributed, these sources are relevant, and this is the next step demonstrated by the prototype.”

TECHNOLOGY AND OFFLINE DESIGN

The implementation uses Python, FastAPI, NumPy, SciPy, JavaScript, browser-based visualization and MediaPipe. A service worker caches resources for offline-first operation.

Offline capability applies to cached local functionality. Optional Grok conversation, speech recognition and speech synthesis require connectivity. Hardware integration, comprehensive offline reliability and medical performance remain validation work.

The prototype is a research demonstration, not a clinically validated diagnostic or treatment product, and is not endorsed by NASA.

INTENDED IMPACT

For space exploration, the project demonstrates how a crew could organize health observations and evidence when communication is delayed or interrupted.

On Earth, the same design could support future research into remote health assistance and home rehabilitation using commodity cameras and wearable devices. These applications would require appropriate clinical evaluation and deployment safeguards.

WHAT A JUDGE CAN TRY IN TWO MINUTES

  1. Open the workstation and select the four mission scenarios.
  2. Open Triage to inspect the Crew Body Map and an emergency vignette.
  3. Open Evidence to inspect an answer, its references and its limitations.
  4. Open Watch + iPhone to explore the companion demonstration.

REUSE, ATTRIBUTION AND AI/SI DISCLOSURE

The joint submission combines AstroKinetics with contributed ASTRA companion material and HUNCH/AURA reference work. The repository identifies original material under MIT and preserves third-party attribution, including BodyParts3D anatomy under CC BY 4.0.

AI/SI tools supported brainstorming, research, data interpretation, coding, debugging, writing, translation, visual design and presentation preparation under human direction. These included Google Antigravity/Gemini, Anthropic Claude Code and OpenAI Codex for contributed ASTRA material.

Machine-learning vision models support the camera workflows. The optional voice assistant uses xAI Grok through ClawAgents. Concept illustrations in the pitch deck were AI-generated. The demonstration video is a recording of the running interface with AI-generated narration from xAI Grok Voice.

The team remains responsible for reviewing the resulting code, scientific claims, references, attribution and generated media. NASA source data, derived material and illustrative demonstration values are distinguished by provenance.
